0.value:
Keeps the last N samples that arrived and sends them all, oldest first, every time a new one comes in.

This turns a stream - one value, or one set of values, per frame - into a tensor of the recent past that other nodes can work on: average it, take its spectrum, find its peak, draw it. Almost any question about "the last second" starts here.

THE OUTPUT IS ALWAYS FULL LENGTH:
From the very first sample the output has N rows. Rows that have not been filled yet are zeros, at the oldest (top) end, and they scroll out as real samples arrive. reset sets every row back to zero.

SAMPLE COUNT IS A TIME WINDOW:
At 60 samples a second, 60 is one second of history and 600 is ten. Longer windows give steadier statistics that react more slowly.

SYNTAX:
t.rolling_buffer <sample count> <dtype> <device>
Default sample count 256, float32, cpu.

EXAMPLE:
t.rolling_buffer 32

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

input:
The sample. Every arrival is stored and the whole buffer sent. A single number is one sample.

reset (button, also an inlet):
Sets every stored value to zero, keeping the shape, and sends the cleared buffer straight away.

sample count (option):
N, the number of samples kept. A change takes effect at the next input: the buffer starts again, empty, at the new length.

update style (option):
"input is stream of samples" (the default) - each number is one sample;
a list of several numbers is several samples, written in order (a list longer than N leaves just its last N). The output is N rows by 1 column. "input is multi-channel sample" - each arrival (a list or 1-D tensor of C values) is ONE sample of C channels; the output is N rows by C columns. A sample with a different C starts a new, empty buffer. "buffer holds one sample of input" - each arrival replaces the whole buffer, which then has the arrival's length.

dtype / device / requires_grad (also inlets):
What the stored tensor is. Incoming data is converted to it. float32 (the default), float16, int64, uint8, bool, complex64 and complex128. The menu also lists the same types under their torch names (torch.float32, float, torch.float ...). There is no float64 here: a float64 NumPy array comes out float32.

OUTPUTS:

output:
A copy of the buffer: N rows, oldest first, newest in the last row.

READING THE DEMO:
Top: make_bump sends a bump 16 values wide that steps one place along every 60 ms. t.rolling_buffer 32, in multi-channel mode, keeps the last 32: one heat_map row per sample, oldest at the top and newest at the bottom, so the moving bump draws a diagonal stripe that scrolls upward. Click reset on the node and the picture empties, then refills from the bottom. Change sample count in the node's options (16, or 64) and the window starts again at that length; the heat_map follows.
Bottom: single random numbers (the default stream mode) gathered into the last 64 (64 rows of 1 column), drawn as a curve with the newest at the right (t.flatten makes the column one row for plot).

RELATED:
t.buffer can also hand back one stored value by position. np.rolling_buffer is the NumPy version; np.sequence records and plays back. capture~ records the audio graph. t.mean and t.rfft are typical next steps.
